headings.title: Introduction to Renal Acid-Base Regulation
headings.content: The human body maintains blood pH within a strict physiological range of 7.35 to 7.45. While the lungs provide rapid regulation by controlling carbon dioxide elimination, the kidneys offer a slower, more powerful, and definitive defense mechanism. The renal system regulates acid-base balance through two primary processes: reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate and excreting fixed metabolic acids. When metabolic acids accumulate, blood pH drops, prompting the kidneys to retain base and eliminate excess hydrogen ions over hours or days.

headings.title: Mechanisms of Hydrogen Ion Secretion and Bicarbonate Rehandling
headings.content: The proximal convoluted tubule is the primary site for reclaiming filtered bicarbonate. Because bicarbonate cannot directly cross the luminal membrane, it combines with secreted hydrogen ions to form carbonic acid. Carbonic anhydrase breaks this down into water and carbon dioxide, which readily diffuse into the tubular cell. Inside the cell, the reaction reverses, generating new bicarbonate that enters the peritubular capillaries alongside active hydrogen secretion.

headings.title: Phosphate and Ammonia Urinary Buffer Systems
headings.content:
- **Phosphate Buffer System**: Filtered hydrogen phosphate captures excess hydrogen ions in the tubular fluid, forming dihydrogen phosphate which is excreted in the urine.
- **Ammonia Buffer System**: Renal tubular cells metabolize glutamine to produce ammonia. Ammonia diffuses into the tubular lumen, binds excess hydrogen ions to form ammonium, and prevents urine pH from dropping below limiting values.

headings.title: Renal Response to Acidosis and Alkalosis
headings.content: During systemic acidosis, the kidneys accelerate hydrogen ion secretion and generate brand new bicarbonate to replenish depleted blood buffers. Conversely, during systemic alkalosis, renal tubular cells decrease hydrogen ion secretion and excrete excess bicarbonate into the urine. This dual adjustment restores the normal plasma bicarbonate-to-carbon dioxide ratio.

headings.title: Clinical Implications and Nursing Assessments
headings.content: Nurses caring for patients with renal impairment must monitor laboratory indicators such as serum bicarbonate, blood pH, and urine output. Renal failure compromises acid excretion, frequently resulting in metabolic acidosis. Clinical assessments include observing respiratory patterns for Kussmaul breathing, checking for electrolyte imbalances like hyperkalemia, and evaluating fluid status.
